fields.definition: A subjective timbre descriptor for a smooth, refined high-frequency character (roughly 5-20 kHz) that stays detailed yet free of harshness, grain, edge, or sibilance, giving the treble a soft, flowing quality.
fields.plain_english: "Silky" means the high notes sound smooth and easy on the ears, with no harsh or scratchy edge. It is like the difference between rough cloth and soft silk.
fields.purpose_function: It names a desirable treble quality so engineers can aim for detailed highs without listener fatigue. It exists to describe the goal of clear yet gentle high frequencies.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may call a vocal or cymbal "silky" after gentle high-shelf EQ, de-essing, or a smooth-sounding mic or preamp, and the word guides gear and EQ choices toward non-fatiguing highs.
common_mistakes: Assuming 'silky' just means more treble; boosting highs can add harshness, which is the opposite of silky.
Confusing 'silky' (smooth, refined highs) with 'dull' (highs rolled off and lacking detail).
Thinking any bright sound is silky, when brightness full of peaks and edge is not silky at all.
scenario_contexts: Describing a lead vocal after gentle de-essing and a smooth high shelf.
Praising the top end of a well-designed condenser or ribbon mic.
Choosing a converter or preamp said to have 'silky' highs for strings or acoustic guitar.

sources: iZotope Learn - A Glossary of Common and Confusing Mixing Terms
ProSoundWeb - Glossary of Commonly Used Sound/Audio Terms
Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook (glossary of descriptive terms)

fields.definition: A mixing descriptor meaning a sound sits clearly at or near the front and upper layer of a mix, audible above the surrounding elements rather than buried within or beneath them.
fields.plain_english: If a sound "sits on top," you can hear it clearly above everything else in the song. It floats on the surface instead of hiding underneath.
fields.purpose_function: It describes good foreground placement in the mix balance so a key part, often the lead vocal, stays present and easy to follow. It exists to talk about where an element lives in the mix's level and front-to-back hierarchy.
fields.practical_application: An engineer raises a fader, adds presence-range EQ, or uses light compression so a vocal sits on top of the band without being buried or too loud.
common_mistakes: Just cranking the fader to make something sit on top, which throws off the overall balance instead of using EQ and compression.
Confusing 'sits on top' (correct foreground balance) with simply being too loud.
Forgetting that carving space in competing tracks can help an element sit on top better than boosting it.
scenario_contexts: Getting a lead vocal to sit on top of a dense rock arrangement.
Placing a lead synth so it sits on top of pads and rhythm parts.
Balancing a snare so its crack sits on top of the drum bus.

sources: iZotope Learn - A Glossary of Common and Confusing Mixing Terms
Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook (mix balance and placement)

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for sound with strong, aggressive dynamic impact, a powerful wall-of-sound punch, usually from drums or a heavily compressed mix, that hits the listener with force.
fields.plain_english: "Slammy" means the sound hits hard and feels powerful, like a punch you can feel in your chest. It often comes from heavy compression on drums.
fields.purpose_function: It names the sensation of forceful impact and loudness-driven energy, helping engineers describe an aggressive, high-impact target sound. It exists to capture the wallop a mix or drum sound delivers.
fields.practical_application: An engineer uses heavy bus or parallel compression plus level to make drums slammy for rock, hip-hop, or EDM, trading some dynamic range for perceived power.
common_mistakes: UNSAFE: Chasing a 'slammy' sound by pushing monitors to very high SPL for long stretches risks hearing damage; keep to safe listening levels and take breaks.
Over-compressing for slam until the mix becomes flat, lifeless, and fatiguing.
Confusing 'slammy' (aggressive impact) with simply loud; slam is about impact, not just level.
scenario_contexts: Making a rock drum bus slammy with parallel compression.
Getting a hip-hop beat to hit slammy on club systems.
Describing an aggressively compressed master that slams.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a loose, imprecise sound that lacks tightness, showing smeared or ill-defined transients, poor timing, or an uncontrolled, boomy low end; it is the opposite of "tight."
fields.plain_english: "Sloppy" means the sound is loose and messy, not clean and controlled. Notes or beats feel smeared together or slightly out of time.
fields.purpose_function: It flags a lack of rhythmic and transient control so the problem can be fixed. It works as the negative counterpart to "tight," pointing to timing or low end that needs cleaning up.
fields.practical_application: On the job a sloppy low end is tightened with EQ, gating, or shorter reverb, while sloppy timing may be fixed by editing, quantizing, or re-tracking.
common_mistakes: Blaming EQ for a sloppy low end when the real cause is loose playing or timing that editing must fix.
Confusing 'sloppy' (loose and uncontrolled) with 'warm' (full but still defined low end).
Over-gating to fix sloppiness and cutting off the natural sustain of notes.
scenario_contexts: A bass part that sounds sloppy because notes ring into each other.
A live kick that is sloppy and boomy in a resonant room.
Describing a rhythm section that plays slightly loose or sloppy.

fields.definition: The blurring or loss of detail and transient definition in a sound, in which distinct events or stereo images run together in time or space; it is commonly caused by phase problems, resonance, excess reverb, or time-domain processing artifacts.
fields.plain_english: "Smear" is when sounds blur together and lose their sharp edges, like a photo that is slightly out of focus. Fine detail and clear timing get lost.
fields.purpose_function: It names a loss of clarity so its cause can be found and reduced. It exists to describe blurred transients or imaging that make a mix less clear and detailed.
fields.practical_application: A technician traces smear to phase misalignment, room resonance, heavy reverb, or linear-phase EQ pre-ringing, then corrects timing, damping, or processing to restore focus.
common_mistakes: Adding lots of reverb without noticing that it smears transients and blurs the mix.
Assuming all EQ is neutral, when linear-phase EQ can smear transients through pre-ringing.
Confusing time smear (blurred transients) with a simple loss of high frequencies.
scenario_contexts: Transients smearing after heavy linear-phase EQ or convolution reverb.
Stereo image smear from a phase problem between two mics.
Low-end smear caused by room resonance blurring bass notes together.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for sound that exhibits smear, with blurred, poorly defined transients or imaging, so detail and clarity are lost and events run together instead of sounding distinct.
fields.plain_english: "Smeary" describes a blurry sound where details run together and nothing is sharp. It is the fuzzy look of a smudged window, but for your ears.
fields.purpose_function: It describes the audible result of smearing so engineers can flag and reduce it. It exists to label a lack of transient and spatial focus.
fields.practical_application: When a mix sounds smeary, a technician reduces reverb, fixes phase, or avoids pre-ringing EQ to sharpen transients and tighten imaging.
common_mistakes: Treating a smeary mix with more EQ when the real fix is less reverb or better phase alignment.
Confusing 'smeary' (blurred detail, a fault) with 'smooth' (pleasantly non-harsh, a good thing).
Not checking in mono, which can reveal phase-related smear that is hidden in stereo.
scenario_contexts: A vocal that turns smeary under too much plate reverb.
A drum bus sounding smeary after aggressive time-domain processing.
Bass and kick sounding smeary together because their transients overlap.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for sound that is easy on the ears and free of harshness, with a flat, even frequency response lacking sharp peaks or dips and with low distortion, especially through the midrange and highs.
fields.plain_english: "Smooth" sound has no harsh or jagged edges. It is easy to listen to for a long time, like a flat, even road with no bumps.
fields.purpose_function: It describes an even, non-fatiguing tonal balance that engineers often aim for. It exists to capture the goal of clean response without harsh peaks.
fields.practical_application: An engineer smooths a track by taming resonant peaks with EQ, lowering distortion, and choosing gear with even response, making it pleasant over long listening.
common_mistakes: Thinking smooth means dull; smooth keeps detail while removing harshness, but dull loses the highs.
Over-smoothing until the mix loses life, presence, and definition.
Confusing a smooth, even response with a scooped one that has real dips in it.
scenario_contexts: Taming a harsh peak near 3 kHz to make a vocal smooth.
Choosing a smooth-sounding EQ or preamp for strings.
Describing a well-balanced master that plays smoothly on many systems.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for sound with fast, well-defined transient attack, a quick and crisp initial snap, typically on drums (especially the snare) or plucked and percussive sounds, giving a tight, articulate leading edge.
fields.plain_english: "Snappy" means the start of each hit is quick and sharp, like the snap of your fingers. You clearly hear the crack at the front of the sound.
fields.purpose_function: It highlights a strong, fast transient so engineers can dial in punch and articulation. It exists to describe a crisp attack that helps a sound cut through and feel tight.
fields.practical_application: An engineer makes a snare snappy with transient shaping, attack-preserving compression, or a small boost around 2-5 kHz, keeping the initial crack intact.
common_mistakes: Using a fast compressor attack that clamps the transient and kills the snap.
Confusing 'snappy' (a fast transient) with 'bright' (extra high-frequency content); they are not the same.
Boosting highs to fake snap instead of preserving the real transient.
scenario_contexts: Shaping a snare to be snappy with a transient designer.
Getting a funk bass to sound snappy and articulate.
Keeping drum overheads snappy by using a slow compressor attack.

fields.definition: A subjective descriptor for a bright, percussive, aggressive transient character, a sharp upper-midrange snap or slap, most often applied to funk or clean electric guitar, snare, or slap bass, combining a crisp attack with cutting brightness.
fields.plain_english: "Spanky" means a sharp, bright, slapping attack, like the crack of a funk guitar chord. The sound has a quick, cutting snap to it.
fields.purpose_function: It describes a lively, cutting mix of transient and brightness that helps percussive parts pop in a mix. It exists to name the spank of aggressive, bright attacks.
fields.practical_application: An engineer gets a clean funk guitar or slap bass spanky with upper-mid and high EQ plus attack-preserving dynamics so it cuts through the groove.
common_mistakes: Adding too much high EQ for spank until the part becomes harsh and thin.
Confusing 'spanky' (a bright percussive attack) with 'warm' (full, rounded low-mids).
Over-compressing and removing the very attack that makes a part spanky.
scenario_contexts: Dialing a clean funk guitar to be spanky in the mix.
Getting slap bass to sound spanky and cut through.
Describing a bright, aggressive snare as spanky.
